**What the statute requires.** Under 83.49(3)(a), a landlord who wants to keep part of a deposit must, within 30 days after the rental agreement ends, give written notice "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505." Your lease ended and you moved out on the same day, so the 30 days ran through 2026-08-30. Your lease (§8) says there is no e-mail agreement. The statute doesn't define "last known mailing address."

**Reading 1: the letter is not the required notice.**
- You gave your new address in writing on 2026-07-28. On this reading, the last known address was the new one, not Apartment 12.
- The landlord then missed the 30-day deadline. Under 83.49(3)(a), it "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant."
- That would mean the full $1,050 comes back to you. The landlord could still sue you for damages afterward.

**Reading 2: the letter counts.**
- It was sent by certified mail, and you actually received it and signed for it. Section 83.505(6) says the e-mail rules do not "preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law."
- The letter also states the amount, the reason, the 15-day warning, and where to send an objection. Those are the contents the statute asks for.
- Under this reading, 83.49(3)(b) applies. If you don't object, the landlord may deduct the $400 and must send you the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice. That date is 2026-09-19, and it has not passed.

**Your objection deadline matters under either reading.** Under 83.49(3)(b), you have 15 days after receiving the notice to object. Counting from 2026-08-27, that is 2026-09-11, and it has not passed. You haven't objected yet. If Reading 2 turns out to be right, a late objection would let the landlord deduct the $400. Even then, 83.49(3)(b) says missing the deadline "does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action."

Your lease (§7) says written notices to the landlord must be delivered by hand to Suite A at 1840 SW 13th Street, or sent there by certified mail. The letter gives the same office address for objections. An objection sent that way by 2026-09-11 is valid under both readings. In it, you can also say the notice went to the wrong address.

**If someone sues,** 83.49(3)(c) says the winning side gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.
